paras: The averted lynching of George Washington took place in Fayette County, Pennsylvania, in February 1903, after Washington, a Black man, was accused of shooting Constable Isaac Hostetler on a passenger train out of Uniontown. Washington was arrested and taken to jail, and a lynching was reported to have been narrowly averted on the way. The only coverage found is a short item in a Morgantown, West Virginia, newspaper.

According to the Morgantown Daily New Dominion, a fight started on a Coal Lick passenger train out of Uniontown, and Washington was put off the train. The paper said he then pulled a gun and fired at Hostetler, the constable at McClellantown, and that two shots took effect, leaving the officer "nearly killed." The item does not say who started the fight or give the date of the shooting.

Washington was arrested and his weapon taken from him, and an officer was sent for from Uniontown to take him to jail. On the way, the paper reported, "a lynching was narrowly averted" because word had spread that he had killed the constable. It did not say who sought to lynch him, how many people were involved, or how the lynching was prevented.
No report of a hearing, indictment or trial for Washington, or of Hostetler's recovery, was found in the coverage.

The Daily New Dominion ran the story on its front page on 28 February 1903 under the headline "OFFICER SHOT. Colored Man in Fayette County Nearly Kills a Constable," and its weekly edition, The New Dominion, reprinted the same text on 4 March. The item opened by noting that Fayette County "has had another shooting affray," called Washington "the negro" in the body, and gave the averted lynching only in its closing sentence, without comment. No Pennsylvania paper's account and no Black-press coverage of the episode were found.

reader.title: Averted lynching of George Washington, Fayette County, Pennsylvania
bases: The only report says a lynching of the arrested man was 'narrowly averted' on the way to jail, with no one killed (A1).
Washington was taken to jail alive; the paper reports only that a lynching was averted because of a report that he had killed the constable, and names no crowd or number (A1).
A single text in the Morgantown Daily New Dominion, repeated verbatim in the same publisher's weekly (A1, A2); no Pennsylvania or Black-press report was found.
